extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of philosophy (esp. Plato/Republic) and instructors seeking an exposition of Books VI–VII
extracted.subtask_description: Expository analysis and paraphrase of Plato's Republic (Books VI–VII), extracting the standards, educational programme, and ideal qualities Plato attributes to guardians/philosophers and the methods of knowledge he proposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guardian's perseverance in search after truth
rubrics_metrics.description: “Of all men the guardian must not faint in the search after truth; he must be prepared to take the longer road, or he will never reach that higher region which is above the four virtues.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guardians (rulers) are required to endure a demanding, extended intellectual effort rather than prefer easy or popular answers; willingness to take the longer, more arduous route toward knowledge is a required quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clear and distinct vision of the virtues
rubrics_metrics.description: “Of the virtues too he must not only get an outline, but a clear and distinct vision.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Superficial familiarity with terms (e.g., justice, temperance) is insufficient; rulers must apprehend the virtues clearly and distinctly, not merely as outlines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Knowledge of the supreme principle (the idea of good)
rubrics_metrics.description: “Ought our guardians then to be ignorant of this supreme principle ... without which no man has any real knowledge of anything?”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guardians must not be ignorant of the 'idea of good'—it is treated as the foundational principle necessary for true knowledge; educational programmes should aim at acquaintance with this principle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preference for reality over mere appearance
rubrics_metrics.description: “A man may desire the appearance of virtue, but he will not desire the appearance of good.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate motives and training by whether they orient the guardian toward genuine goodness and reality rather than towards mere displays or semblances of virtue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understanding the idea of good as cause of knowledge and being
rubrics_metrics.description: “That which is the sun of intelligent natures, is the idea of good, the cause of knowledge and truth, yet other and fairer than they are, and standing in the same relation to them in which the sun stands to light.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The ideal ruler should grasp the metaphysical role of the Good: as the source of truth/knowledge and as analogous to the sun; this is a central conceptual target of education.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between visible and intelligible worlds (line analogy)
rubrics_metrics.description: “Imagine further their corresponding worlds—one of the visible, the other of the intelligible; ... figure the distinction under the image of a line divided into two unequal parts, and may again subdivide each part into two lesser segments representative of the stages of knowledge in either sphere.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Knowledge should be classified along this visible/intelligible axis and subdivided into stages; curricula and assessments should recognize different epistemic levels (shadows/reflections, natural objects, mathematics/hypotheses, and pure ideas).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mapping faculties to stages of knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: “To those four divisions of knowledge you may assign four corresponding faculties—pure intelligence to the highest sphere; active intelligence to the second; to the third, faith; to the fourth, the perception of shadows...”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess learners and intellectual tasks by which faculty they exercise (from perception of shadows up to pure intelligence) and expect increasing clearness to track the truth of objects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical sciences as preparatory steps/ladders
rubrics_metrics.description: “The steps of the ladder leading up to this highest or universal existence are the mathematical sciences, which also contain in themselves an element of the universal. They then cease to be hypotheses or pictures, and become essential parts of a higher truth...”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mathematics and number-calculation are prescribed as essential preparatory disciplines to train the mind for abstraction and ascent to higher truths; they are instrumental rather than ends in themselves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hierarchy of knowledge: hypotheses vs. dialectic
rubrics_metrics.description: “In [mathematics] the mind works with figures and numbers ... used as hypotheses without being analysed. Whereas in the other division reason uses the hypotheses as stages or steps in the ascent to the idea of good ... and finally resting in them.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate between knowledge that uses hypotheses instrumentally (mathematics) and dialectical reason that analyzes and integrates hypotheses into first principles; educational expectations differ for each.

rubrics_metrics.name: Philosopher's moral character and temperament
rubrics_metrics.description: “He has the noblest gifts of nature, and makes the highest use of them. All his desires are absorbed in the love of wisdom, which is the love of truth. None of the graces of a beautiful soul are wanting in him; neither can he fear death, or think much of human life.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The ideal philosopher-ruler combines intellectual excellence with noble character: devotion to truth, disinterest in personal honors, courage regarding death, and a harmonious soul—these are criteria for selection and evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modern philosopher's adjusted role
rubrics_metrics.description: “The philosopher in modern times is one who fixes his mind on the laws of nature in their sequence and connexion, not on fragments or pictures of nature; on history, not on controversy; on the truths which are acknowledged by the few, not on the opinions of the many.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contemporary philosophical activity is judged by attentiveness to systematic laws, historical understanding, classification by nature, and focus on recognized truths—less the ancient visionary method; curricula should reflect these priorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations of the Socratic (negative/interrogative) method
rubrics_metrics.description: “The negative and interrogative method of Socrates must be superseded by a positive and constructive one.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While Socratic questioning reveals ignorance, it may not build comprehensive systems; instruction and evaluation should include constructive synthesis as well as critique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explanation for philosophers' social uselessness or corruption
rubrics_metrics.description: “The uselessness of philosophers is explained by the circumstance that mankind will not use them... Concerning the false philosopher, Socrates argues that the best is most liable to corruption; and that the finer nature is more likely to suffer from alien conditions.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand and evaluate the social reception of philosophers: either ignored, feared, or corrupted by public institutions; selection and training should account for social pressures and the need for congenial environments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for congenial conditions for highest natures
rubrics_metrics.description: “In general a man can only receive his highest development in a congenial state or family, among friends or fellow-workers.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessments of potential and success should consider social/contextual fit: outstanding natures require supportive milieus to flourish; failure may reflect environment more than individual defect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risk and potential of adverse circumstances to produce reformers or destructives
rubrics_metrics.description: “He may sometimes be stirred by adverse circumstances to such a degree that he rises up against them and reforms them... in a few instances ... may break away entirely from the world ... sometimes into great good, sometimes into great evil.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that adverse conditions can both crush and catalyze greatness; selection and policy must weigh this unpredictability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public ignorance of true philosophy; prevalence of imitators
rubrics_metrics.description: “They have only known a conventional imitation of philosophy, words without thoughts, systems which have no life in them... the same double feeling respecting the mass of mankind has always existed.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Educational and civic programs should aim to distinguish authentic philosophical education from mere rhetorical or conventional imitation; public pedagogy matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ideal method of knowledge as inference from whole to parts; consistency as test of truth
rubrics_metrics.description: “He would probably have described his method as proceeding by regular steps to a system of universal knowledge, which inferred the parts from the whole rather than the whole from the parts... consistency is the test of truth.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plato's ideal epistemic method is synthetic and holistic; evaluation of theories should emphasize internal consistency and systematic integration over piecemeal induction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cave allegory as standard for education/conversion
rubrics_metrics.description: “I will describe in a figure the enlightenment or unenlightenment of our nature:—Imagine human beings living in an underground den ... they see only the shadows ... suppose you suddenly turn them round ... make them look with pain and grief to themselves at the real images ... dragged up a steep and rugged ascent into the presence of the sun ... How will they rejoice in passing from darkness to light!”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Education is characterized as conversion: turning the soul toward the light, a painful and gradual process; pedagogical success is measured by the capacity to re-orient perception toward truth, not merely teaching facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conversion not equivalent to giving eyes; faculty already present
rubrics_metrics.description: “Some persons fancy that instruction is like giving eyes to the blind, but we say that the faculty of sight was always there, and that the soul only requires to be turned round towards the light. And this is conversion; other virtues are almost like bodily habits, and may be acquired in the same manner, but intelligence has a diviner life, and is indestructible...”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instruction should be evaluated by whether it effects conversion (a re-orientation), recognizing innate capacities rather than assuming creation ex nihilo; different virtues require different modes of cultivation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Philosopher-rulers must descend to govern; rulers must not be desirous to rule
rubrics_metrics.description: “Those who rule must not be those who are desirous to rule; ... the philosopher ... must no longer live in the heaven of ideas. You must, each of you, take your turn, and become able to use your eyes in the dark ... you will be forced down again among the captives in the den to partake of their labours and honours.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Selection criteria: choose philosophers likely to ascend to knowledge but who can also be compelled to re-enter political life; rulers should be reluctant to rule yet capable of governing for the common good.

rubrics_metrics.name: Educational curriculum for rulers: gymnastic and music insufficient; number required
rubrics_metrics.description: “Our former education had two branches, gymnastic, which was occupied with the body, and music ... but neither of these sciences gave any promise of doing what we want. Nothing remains to us but that universal or primary science of which all the arts and sciences are partakers, I mean number or calculation.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design of ruling-class education prioritizes mathematical training (number/calculation) as the central, universal discipline that prepares the soul for higher knowledge; physical and literary training alone are inadequate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Number as stimulant and conductor to thought and being
rubrics_metrics.description: “Number, in my view, is rather to be regarded as a conductor to thought and being... All number has also an elevating effect; it raises the mind out of the foam and flux of generation to the contemplation of being... The retail use is not required by us; ... number is to be regarded as a conductor to thought and being.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mathematical exercises are valued not for practical arithmetic but for their capacity to stimulate abstraction, detect relations (unity/plurality), and elevate the mind; evaluate math education by its formative, not merely utilitarian, effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of contradictions and relations in perception to prompt abstraction
rubrics_metrics.description: “Things sensible are of two kinds; the one class invite or stimulate the mind, while in the other the mind acquiesces. ... The stimulating class are the things which suggest contrast and relation ... the perception of their contrast or relation quickens and sets in motion the mind, which is puzzled by the confused intimations of sense, and has recourse to number...”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pedagogical strategies should exploit perceptual contrasts and relational problems that compel the mind to abstract; assessment should look for capacity to move from sense-confusion to numerical/abstract resolution.
